Chemical equations, empirical and molecular formulae, percentage composition

summary: 1 u = 1/12 of the mass of a ¹²C atom = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁴ g; relative atomic and molecular masses are unitless ratios; the tabulated atomic mass is an isotope-weighted average.
Formulae come from valencies by criss-cross; learn the radicals with their charges, and remember Hg₂²⁺ (Hg₂Cl₂), S₂O₃²⁻ and Cr₂O₇²⁻.
Percentage of an element = (atoms × A_r)/M × 100; urea is 46.7 % N, CuSO₄·5H₂O is 36.1 % water.
Empirical formula: % → ÷ A_r → ÷ smallest → whole numbers; molecular formula = n × empirical formula, with M = 2 × VD.
Lavoisier (mass), Proust (definite), Dalton (multiple), Richter (reciprocal), Gay-Lussac (gas volumes), Avogadro (equal volumes, equal molecules).
Dalton's indivisibility and identical-mass postulates failed (subatomic particles, isotopes, isobars); conservation of atoms in chemical change survives.
One mole = 6.022 × 10²³ entities (exact since 2019) = M grams = 22.4 L of gas at STP; n = m/M = N/NA = V/22.4.
Limiting reactant = smallest moles ÷ coefficient; it fixes the product. % yield = actual/theoretical × 100.
terms: Atomic mass unit and relative atomic mass

sections.title: Rutherford's and Bohr's atomic models; the spectrum of hydrogen
de Broglie's equation and Heisenberg's uncertainty principle
Orbitals and quantum numbers; Aufbau, Pauli and Hund; electronic configuration

summary: Rutherford: most of the atom is empty; positive charge and mass sit in a nucleus about 10⁻¹⁵ m across. The model fails on stability and on line spectra.
Bohr: stationary orbits with mvr = nh/2π; photons only on jumps, Δ E = hν. For one-electron species r ∝ n^2/Z, v ∝ Z/n, E = -13.6 Z^2/n^2 eV.
Hydrogen lines obey 1/λ = RH(1/n1^2 - 1/n2^2): Lyman (UV), Balmer (visible), Paschen, Brackett, Pfund (IR). A sample falling from level n gives n(n-1)/2 lines.
de Broglie: λ = h/mv; significant only for tiny masses; 2π r = nλ gives Bohr's rule.
Heisenberg: Δ x·Δ p ≥ h/4π, so orbits give way to orbitals (probability regions).
Quantum numbers n, l (0 to n − 1), m (−l to +l), s (±½); radial nodes n − l − 1, angular nodes l.
Aufbau by (n + l), Pauli (two electrons per orbital, opposite spins), Hund (no pairing until each degenerate orbital has one). Cr 3d⁵ 4s¹ and Cu 3d¹⁰ 4s¹; ions lose 4s before 3d.

sections.title: Modern periodic law and table; s, p, d and f blocks; isoelectronic species
Periodic trends: size, ionisation energy, electronegativity, electron affinity and metallic character

summary: Modern periodic law: properties are periodic functions of atomic number; periodicity comes from the recurrence of similar outer configurations.
7 periods (2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32 elements) and 18 groups; s, p, d and f blocks by the subshell that takes the last electron; He is s-block but sits in group 18.
Group from configuration: s-block ns electrons, p-block 10 + ns + np, d-block ns + (n − 1)d.
Isoelectronic species share an electron count; their radius falls as Z rises.
Across a period Z_eff rises: size falls; IE, EA and electronegativity rise; metallic character and basic character of oxides fall. Down a group the reverse.
IE exceptions Be > B, N > O (Mg > Al, P > S); EA exceptions Cl > F, S > O; noble gases, Be, Mg and N have near-zero or negative EA.
Highest IE He, lowest Cs; most electronegative F (4.0); highest EA Cl. A big jump in successive IEs counts the valence electrons.
Ga < Al in size (poor 3d shielding); Zr ≈ Hf (lanthanoid contraction).

sections.title: Electronic theory of valency; ionic, covalent and coordinate bonds; Lewis structures
VSEPR theory and shapes; valence bond theory, σ and π bonds, hybridisation

summary: Atoms bond to reach a noble-gas configuration: ionic (transfer), covalent (sharing), coordinate (a pair donated by one atom — NH₄⁺, H₃O⁺, H₃N→BF₃). The octet rule fails for BF₃, PCl₅, SF₆, NO and xenon fluorides.
Formal charge = V − L − B/2; the best Lewis structure minimises formal charges.
VSEPR: shape from the steric number SN = ½(V + M − c + a); lp–lp > lp–bp > bp–bp squeezes angles: CH₄ 109.5° > NH₃ 107° > H₂O 104.5°.
Lone pairs in a trigonal bipyramid go equatorial: SF₄ see-saw, ClF₃ T-shaped, XeF₂ linear; XeF₄ is square planar.

σ bonds come from head-on overlap, π bonds from sideways overlap; double = σ + π, triple = σ + 2π. Hybridisation sp, sp², sp³, sp³d, sp³d², sp³d³ for SN 2–7; more s character, shorter and stronger bond.
μ = q × d (debye); symmetric molecules have μ = 0; NH₃ > NF₃; % ionic character = μ(obs)/(e × d) × 100. Fajans: small, highly charged cations and large anions raise covalent character.
Bond length falls as bond order and s character rise; resonance makes equivalent bonds equal.

Hydrogen bonds (F, O, N) explain the high boiling points of H₂O, HF and NH₃, ice floating and o-nitrophenol's volatility; metallic bonds are an electron sea; London forces grow with size and surface area.

topics: Classical and electronic concepts of oxidation and reduction; oxidation number

sections.title: Classical and electronic concepts of oxidation and reduction; oxidation number
Balancing redox equations by the oxidation-number and ion-electron methods; applications

summary: Classical: oxidation = addition of O or an electronegative element, removal of H or an electropositive element; reduction the reverse.
Electronic: oxidation = loss of electrons, reduction = gain; the oxidant is reduced and the reductant oxidised; both always occur together.
Oxidation number rules: free element 0; F −1; O −2 except peroxides (−1), superoxides (−½) and OF₂ (+2); H +1 except metal hydrides (−1); the sum equals the charge.
Watch the traps: Fe₃O₄ +8/3, S₄O₆²⁻ +2.5, CrO₅ and H₂S₂O₈ +6 (peroxide links), OsO₄ +8, NH₄NO₃ −3 and +5.
Highest oxidation state → only an oxidant; lowest → only a reductant; intermediate → both, and able to disproportionate (H₂O₂, Cl₂ in alkali, Cu⁺, HNO₂).
Balancing: equalise the total change in oxidation number, or add half-reactions after balancing O with H₂O, H with H⁺ (OH⁻ in base) and charge with electrons.
n-factors: MnO₄⁻ 5 (acid), 3 (neutral), 1 (strong base); Cr₂O₇²⁻ 6; moles react in the inverse ratio of n-factors.

summary: Kinetic theory: random elastic motion, no attractions, negligible molecular volume; KE = (3/2)RT per mole for every gas; urms = √3RT/M and ump : uav : urms = 1 : 1.128 : 1.224.
Boyle, Charles, pressure and Avogadro laws combine into PV = nRT (R = 8.314 J or 0.0821 L atm mol⁻¹ K⁻¹); always use kelvin.
Dalton: pi = xiP; Graham: rate ∝ 1/√M (lighter gases diffuse faster; time ∝ √M).
Real gases: Z = PV/nRT; van der Waals a (attraction) and b (excluded volume); ideal behaviour at low P and high T; large a means easy liquefaction.
Vapour pressure depends only on the liquid and T; boiling occurs when VP = external pressure. Surface tension (N m⁻¹) and liquid viscosity (Pa s) fall as T rises.
Liquid crystals (nematic, smectic, cholesteric) flow but keep orientational order; used in LCDs and thermometers. Solubility curves show crystallisation yields; KNO₃ rises steeply, NaCl barely.
Crystalline solids: long-range order, sharp mp, anisotropic; amorphous: short-range order, soften over a range, isotropic. Efflorescent loses water; deliquescent dissolves; hygroscopic absorbs.
7 crystal systems, 14 Bravais lattices; sc, bcc, fcc have Z = 1, 2, 4 and CN 6, 8, 12; ρ = ZM/(a³N_A). Solids are ionic, covalent network, molecular or metallic.

sections.title: Physical and chemical equilibrium; law of mass action; Kc, Kp and Q
Le Chatelier's principle and its applications
Arrhenius, Brønsted–Lowry and Lewis acids and bases; Ostwald's dilution law
Ionic product of water, pH, pOH, pKa, pKb; common-ion effect; solubility product
Acidic and basic buffers; types of salts and their hydrolysis

summary: At dynamic equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal and concentrations are constant, but both reactions continue; a catalyst only shortens the time taken to get there.
Kc and Kp take products over reactants with each concentration raised to its coefficient; pure solids and pure liquids are omitted because their concentrations are constant.
Kp = Kc(RT)^Δ n. When Δ n = 0 the two are equal and both are dimensionless; when Δ n = -2, Kc carries L² mol⁻² and Kp atm⁻².
Q is the same ratio at any moment: Q < K shifts forward, Q > K shifts backward. Only temperature changes K; pressure shifts the position only if Δ n ≠ 0.

Le Chatelier: added reactant, removed product, higher pressure (towards fewer gas moles) and lower temperature (for an exothermic reaction) all push the equilibrium forward. Haber, contact and Ostwald each use a compromise temperature of roughly 700–800 K for rate, with pressure chosen from Δ n.
Arrhenius: H⁺/OH⁻ in water. Brønsted–Lowry: proton donor/acceptor, with conjugate pairs differing by one H⁺. Lewis: electron-pair acceptor/donor. Amphiprotic species (H₂O, HCO₃⁻) can act either way.
Ostwald's dilution law gives α = √Ka/C: dilution raises the fraction dissociated but lowers [H^+] = √KaC.
Kw = 10^-14 at 25 °C, pH + pOH = 14, pKa + pKb = 14. Neutral is pH 7 only at 25 °C.
terms: Law of mass action (Guldberg and Waage, 1864)

units.title: Volumetric Analysis
topics: Equivalent weight; concentration as percentage, g/L, normality, molarity, molality, formality, ppm, ppb and mole fraction
Primary and secondary standards; the law of equivalence and the normality equation

sections.title: Equivalent weight and every concentration unit
Primary and secondary standards; the law of equivalence

summary: Volumetric analysis measures the volume of a standard solution needed to react completely with a measured volume of analyte; the end point is the indicator's approximation to the equivalence point.
Equivalent weight E = M/n; the n-factor is the basicity of an acid, the acidity of a base, the cation charge of a salt, or the electron change of an oxidant or reductant.
KMnO₄ has three equivalent weights because it is reduced to Mn²⁺ (n = 5), MnO₂ (n = 3) or MnO₄²⁻ (n = 1); K₂Cr₂O₇ is always n = 6.
Molarity is per litre of solution and changes with temperature; molality is per kilogram of solvent and does not. Normality = molarity × n-factor.
M = 10 × %w/w × d / MB is the only conversion that needs the density; ppm and ppb are mass ratios, and mole fractions sum to 1.
Dilution conserves moles: M1V1 = M2V2.
A primary standard is pure, stable, non-hygroscopic, soluble, fast-reacting and of high molar mass; NaOH, HCl, KMnO₄, Na₂S₂O₃ and I₂ are secondary standards and must be standardised.
At the equivalence point N1V1 = N2V2, and equivalents can be counted as NV, mass/E, or n-factor × moles.

sections.title: Rate of reaction, rate expressions, the rate constant and its units; order and molecularity
Integrated rate laws and half-lives of zero- and first-order reactions
Collision theory, activation and threshold energy, the activated complex; factors affecting rate; catalysis

summary: Rate is positive: for a reactant rate = -(1/a)d[R]/dt; the coefficient of every species must be included. Average rate is a chord, instantaneous rate a tangent.
The rate law is experimental; order is the sum of the exponents and may be 0, fractional or negative, while molecularity is a theoretical whole number for one step.
Units of k: mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹ (0), s⁻¹ (1), L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹ (2), L² mol⁻² s⁻¹ (3).
Zero order: [A] = [A]0 - kt, t1/2 = [A]0/2k (doubles when [A]0 doubles), and the reaction finishes at [A]0/k.
First order: ln([A]0/[A]) = kt, [A] = [A]0e^-kt, t1/2 = 0.693/k — independent of [A]0; n half-lives leave (1/2)^n.
A straight ln[A]–t plot (slope -k) is the test for first order; a straight [A]–t plot is the test for zero order.
Collision theory: rate depends on collision frequency and on the fraction of collisions with energy ≥ threshold energy and correct orientation; the activated complex is the top of the barrier.
k = Ae^-Ea/RT; a 10 °C rise roughly doubles the rate; the barrier itself does not fall with temperature.
terms: Threshold energy, activation energy and activated complex

sections.title: Electrolytic cells and the qualitative and quantitative laws of electrolysis
Standard electrode potential, the SHE and the calomel electrode, and the electrochemical series
Galvanic cells and their standard emf; primary, secondary and hydrogen–oxygen fuel cells

summary: An electrolytic cell uses electrical energy to drive a non-spontaneous reaction; the anode is positive and the cathode negative, but oxidation is at the anode and reduction at the cathode in every cell.

Products of electrolysis follow preferential discharge: the ion with the higher E^° is reduced at the cathode; with inert electrodes in water, O₂ appears at the anode unless a concentrated halide gives Cl₂, Br₂ or I₂.
Faraday's first law: m = ZIt with Z = E/96 500; second law: m1/m2 = E1/E2, and one faraday deposits one gram equivalent.
E^° is a reduction potential measured against the SHE (0.00 V; 1 M H⁺, 1 atm H₂, 298 K, Pt black); the calomel electrode is a portable secondary reference at about 0.24 V.
The electrochemical series gives reactivity, displacement, cell emf and electrolysis products; higher E^° gains electrons, lower E^° loses them.
E^°cell = E^°cathode - E^°anode; positive means spontaneous; E^° is intensive, so doubling a half-reaction leaves it unchanged.
Nernst: E = E^° - (0.059/n)log Q at 298 K; Δ G^° = -nFE^°; at equilibrium E = 0 and E^° = (0.059/n)log K.
Primary cells (dry cell 1.5 V, alkaline) cannot be recharged; secondary cells (lead–acid 2 V per cell, lithium-ion) can; fuel cells (H₂–O₂) run continuously and give only water.

sections.title: Systems and surroundings; state functions; internal energy; intensive and extensive properties; the first law and enthalpy

summary: A system is open, closed or isolated; only an isolated system has Δ U = 0 always. U, H, S and G are state functions; q and w are path functions whose sum alone is fixed.
Extensive properties scale with amount (mass, U, H, S, G); intensive ones do not (T, P, density, molar enthalpy).
First law (IUPAC): Δ U = q + w, with q positive into the system and w = -PΔ V positive when work is done on it. An expanding gas has negative work.
H = U + PV; Δ H = qp at constant pressure and Δ U = qv at constant volume; Δ H = Δ U + Δ ng RT.
Δ Hf^° is zero only for an element in its standard state; Δ H^°rxn is products minus reactants.
Combustion is always exothermic; neutralisation of a strong acid by a strong base is −57.1 kJ mol⁻¹; fusion and vaporisation are always endothermic, and Δ Hsub = Δ Hfus + Δ Hvap.
Laplace's law: reversing a reaction reverses the sign of Δ H. Hess's law: Δ H is path-independent, so equations can be added, reversed and multiplied.
Second law: Δ Suniverse > 0 for a spontaneous change; Δ Ssurr = -Δ H/T, so an exothermic reaction can be spontaneous even when its own entropy falls.
terms: Hess's law of constant heat summation

summary: Write the two bookkeeping integers (A, Z) honestly and every nuclear equation, including series staircases of a dozen steps, falls into place.
Stability is geography: inside the neutron-bending belt (magic addresses preferred) nuclei endure; outside, β-decays walk them home and the heavies shed α-particles.
Bombardment extends the map: artificial transmutation and induced radioactivity brew the isotopes that medicine and industry now order by catalogue.
Carbon-14 is the belt's most famous emigrant: made in the sky, eaten by everything alive, and read back as a 50 000-year clock.

summary: Hydrogen's personas scale in reducing violence (H₂ < [H] < atomic H); its isotopes give heavy water (a moderator) and tritium (a tracer).

Oxides sort by character — acidic, basic, amphoteric, neutral, peroxide, superoxide, mixed — and ozone is oxygen's bent, resonating, oxidizing allotrope, whose stratospheric veil CFC chemistry taught us to defend.
Ammonia is base and ligand in one lone pair; phosphine its feebler, fouler sibling; nitric acid an oxidizing acid whose product gas advertises its concentration.
Halogens weaken downwards as oxidants while their hydrides strengthen as acids and reductants; HF alone is weak — and alone eats glass.

Carbon reinvents itself from diamond to graphene; CO poisons quietly and refines metals; the sulphur trio H₂S/SO₂/H₂SO₄ escalates from analytical precipitant to the dehydrating, oxidizing king of chemicals.

summary: Ores are concentrated (flotation owns the sulphides), converted to oxides (calcination without air, roasting with it), then reduced by the cheapest agent the Ellingham ladder allows — carbon for the middle class, electricity for the aristocrats, self-reduction for copper and mercury.
Refining polishes with green poles, electric baths and moving molten zones; impurities are sorted by the same electrochemical series that runs the cells.
The s-block supplies sodium's industrial trio (metal, hydroxide, carbonate) by Downs, chlor-alkali and Solvay routes, and calcium's lime cycle closes on itself.
Transition metals wear complexes whose colours, spins and geometries crystal-field splitting predicts — from tetraammine blue to chemotherapy's cisplatin.

Iron's blast furnace and the two steel converters turn carbon content into a dial (pig ≫ cast > steel > wrought), while rust — a wet electrochemical cell — is fought by smarter neighbours: zinc above all.

summary: Macro- and microminerals differ in required amount, not in importance; chemical form and dose decide benefit or harm.
Na⁺ dominates extracellular fluid, K⁺ dominates cytosol, Mg²⁺ partners ATP and chlorophyll, and Ca²⁺ combines a structural role in bone with rapid signalling roles.
Zn²⁺ is a redox-inert catalytic/structural ion; Fe and Cu handle oxygen and electrons but must be protein-bound; cobalt reaches human metabolism through microbially made vitamin B₁₂.
Nickel has established roles in plants and microbes, while chromium(III)'s supposed essential role in humans remains unproved; chromium(VI) is an important carcinogen.
Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase is the primary-active 3-out/2-in pump. SGLTs spend the Na⁺ gradient, not ATP directly, to import glucose.
Oral rehydration works because intestinal SGLT1 links glucose uptake to Na⁺ and water absorption.
Iron overload produces hydroxyl radicals; arsenic blocks thiol enzymes and imitates phosphate; organic mercury biomagnifies and crosses into brain and fetus.
Lead injures the developing nervous system without an identified safe childhood threshold, while cadmium accumulates in kidney and secondarily destroys bone.

summary: Carbon's tetravalency, strong self-linking and multiple bonding create an enormous set of stable molecular architectures.
Functional groups and homologous series convert that diversity into learnable families; alkyl, aryl and benzyl must be distinguished by where the free valence lies.
Degree of unsaturation counts rings plus π bonds and is the fastest check before drawing or naming structures.
IUPAC names are built by seniority, parent selection, low-locant numbering and alphabetical assembly.
Structural isomers differ in connectivity; stereoisomers keep connectivity but differ in arrangement. E/Z, enantiomers, diastereomers, racemates and meso forms each answer a different question.
Homolysis makes radicals, heterolysis makes ions. Curly arrows track electron pairs from nucleophile to electrophile.
Alkyl donation and hyperconjugation stabilize carbocations/radicals but destabilize carbanions; resonance can dominate all three.
Inductive effects fade through σ bonds, while resonance operates only where p orbitals overlap; acid/base and intermediate-strength orders usually reveal which effect controls the system.

summary: Refineries crack long chains, pyrolyse feedstocks to light alkenes and reform straight chains into branched/aromatic molecules that engines and polymer plants actually want.
Octane rewards resistance to autoignition; cetane rewards prompt compression ignition. Molecular shape therefore wins opposite prizes in the two fuels.
Alkanes are strong-σ, nonpolar and slow to react except by combustion and radical pathways; ethane exemplifies combustion, UV substitution and cracking.
Alkenes spend a π bond in addition reactions. Carbocation stability explains Markovnikov orientation, while peroxide changes HBr addition into a radical anti-Markovnikov process.
Alkynes can be stopped at a cis- or trans-alkene by choosing the reduction system; their terminal C–H is acidic because an sp conjugate base is comparatively stable.
Benzene is stabilized by a six-electron cyclic π system (Hückel 4n+2), so electrophiles substitute a ring hydrogen rather than permanently adding and destroying aromaticity.

Ethers: Williamson synthesis and properties of diethyl ether

summary: Monohaloalkanes react through a mechanistic fork: unhindered substrates invite concerted SN2 backside attack, while cation-stabilizing substrates ionize in SN1; bases and heat open the elimination side-road.
The leaving-group order RI > RBr > RCl >> RF and the aqueous/alcoholic KOH distinction settle a large share of conversion questions.

Chloroform's examination identity is haloform preparation, phosgene formation in air and dichlorocarbene reactions; chlorobenzene's is a strong aryl C–Cl bond that refuses ordinary substitution until Dow conditions.
Alcohols combine hydrogen bonding with four reaction exits — alkoxide formation, substitution, dehydration and oxidation — whose class orders identify 1°, 2° and 3° alcohols.
Hydroboration–oxidation and hydration are regiochemical opposites, the oxo process adds a carbon before reduction, and fermentation is enzyme-limited ethanol production.
Phenol's acidity and ring activation both flow from conjugation with the ring: phenoxide is stabilized, NaHCO₃ is not decomposed, and bromine water gives instant tribromination.
Williamson synthesis succeeds when the SN2 partner is chosen as the less hindered halide; diethyl ether is a useful inert solvent whose peroxide formation is its defining hazard.

summary: Aldehydes and ketones are distinguished by oxidation behaviour, not by 2,4-DNP: aldehydes reduce Tollens' reagent; ordinary ketones do not.
Controlled stopping power is the theme of preparation — PCC stops at aldehyde, poisoned Pd stops Rosenmund at aldehyde, and soft organometallics stop at ketone.
Enolate chemistry at the α-carbon gives aldol products and the haloform reaction; blocking α-H switches an aldehyde to Cannizzaro disproportionation.
Benzaldehyde combines an aldehyde's Tollens response with aromatic specialities: no Fehling reaction, Cannizzaro, benzoin and Perkin condensations.
Carboxylic acids owe their acidity and high boiling points to carboxylate resonance and hydrogen-bonded dimers; substituent effects and HVZ chemistry operate through that same functional group.
Formic acid breaks the family pattern by reducing mild oxidants and dehydrating to CO.
Acyl derivatives react by addition–elimination in the order chloride > anhydride > ester > amide; easy conversions run down that ladder.
Saponification, Claisen condensation and Hofmann bromamide degradation are the derivative reactions most likely to be recognized by product and carbon count.

summary: The nitro group withdraws electrons, acidifies an α-C–H and can be reduced all the way to an amine or stopped/dimerized at intermediate oxidation levels by choosing the medium.
Nitrobenzene's ring is deactivated and meta-directing, in complete contrast to the aniline produced from it.
Primary-amine synthesis is an exercise in carbon bookkeeping: nitrile reduction extends, Hofmann degradation shortens, and Gabriel protects nitrogen from over-alkylation.
Aqueous basicity balances alkyl donation against solvation; resonance makes aniline and especially p-nitroaniline feeble bases.
Hoffmann and Hinsberg separations exploit the presence or absence of N–H bonds; nitrous acid and the carbylamine reaction identify amine class in test tubes.
Diazotization converts aniline into a versatile leaving group for phenols, haloarenes and azo dyes, while ring protection tames aniline for controlled substitution.
Organometallic carbon is nucleophilic: lithium gives force, magnesium gives generality, and copper/cadmium give the selectivity needed to stop at ketones or form chosen C–C bonds.

summary: A viable process joins reaction chemistry to separation, recycle, energy, quality and waste systems; batch suits variety, continuous suits volume.
Cement clinker minerals and gypsum explain strength and setting, while limestone calcination makes process CO₂ unavoidable without substitution/capture.
Kraft pulping's chemical-recovery loop is why a paper mill can be both a fibre factory and a power station.
Haber, Ostwald, Contact, chlor-alkali, Solvay and urea each compress to one catalyst/reagent, one equilibrium trick and one product-separation trick.
Uses of common substances are predictable from properties such as conductivity, oxide passivation, alkalinity, π reactivity and hydrogen bonding.
Addition versus condensation polymerization, chromophore/auxochrome design and drug action classes organize the consumer-chemical world.
Fertilizer value is printed as N–P₂O₅–K₂O; pesticide persistence and nutrient runoff are the environmental price of careless dosage.
Tyndall scattering identifies colloids, iCRT prices osmosis from saline drips to desalination, and bicarbonate keeps blood near pH 7.4.

summary: Anion analysis begins with acid-evolved gases and ends with precipitate confirmations whose acid/ammonia solubilities separate look-alikes.
Cation groups are solubility cliffs climbed in order; group reagents work because pH controls S²⁻, OH⁻ and CO₃²⁻ availability.
Organic tests are the functional-group reactions of Chapters 17–20 read backwards from product to structure, with benzene and phenol as the standing bromine-test traps.
Lassaigne's fusion converts covalent N, S and halogens into CN⁻, S²⁻ and X⁻ so inorganic colour chemistry can see them.
Molisch, Benedict, iodine, Biuret, ninhydrin and grease-spot tests identify the three great food classes by their reactive groups.
Separation choice is property choice: volatility for distillation, solubility for crystallization, partition for chromatography and √M for atmolysis.
An indicator is chosen from the pH of the salt at equivalence, not from habit; the end point is an observation that must be engineered onto the equivalence point.
Permanganate counts five electrons in acid and announces itself; iodine methods split into direct iodimetry and indirect iodometry with late starch.
